explanation:
# CrossFit Fran: Benchmark Times & Performance Levels

Fran is CrossFit's most famous benchmark WOD: **21-15-9 reps of thrusters and pull-ups, for time** — 45 reps of each movement, 90 in total. It's a sprint, not a grind: the whole workout lasts only a few minutes, which makes it a clean, repeatable benchmark. Same two movements, same rep scheme, every time — this year's time is directly comparable to last year's.

## Rx Loads by Category

| Category | Thrusters | Pull-ups |
|---|---|---|
| Men Rx | 95 lb (43 kg) | Strict or kipping pull-ups |
| Women Rx | 65 lb (29 kg) | Strict or kipping pull-ups |
| Scaled (both) | 75/55 lb or less | Jumping pull-ups / banded |

The bar starts from the front rack, not the floor. The thruster is a front squat plus overhead press in one continuous movement; the pull-up requires the chin over the bar.

## How Your Level Is Calculated

The calculator takes your time in seconds (example: 300 = 5:00) and places it within the following bands, established by the CrossFit community and validated by Open and Sanctional competition results:

- **Elite**: under 2:30 — a competition-grade cardiovascular engine, unbroken sets or minimal planned breaks.
- **Advanced**: 2:30 – 3:00 — strong thrusters, nearly unbroken pull-ups.
- **Intermediate**: 3:00 – 5:00 — where most consistent CrossFitters land.
- **Beginner**: 5:00 – 8:00 — Rx loads but breaking sets frequently.
- **Scaled**: modified loads or movements (see table above).

A realistic first Rx Fran for most box members is **5–8 minutes**. Sub-3:00 is genuinely fast; sub-2:30 is rare outside competitive athletes. For reference: Rich Froning set 2:13 in competition; the documented men's record sits around **1:53** (Hunter McIntyre, 2019, verified competition conditions).

## Why Fran Is Hard — The Real Limiter

The limiter is rarely strength: 43 kg on the thruster is light for most intermediate CrossFitters. The problem is **cardiovascular recovery between sets** plus grip and pulling endurance. The thruster spikes heart rate disproportionately because it combines an energetically expensive leg movement with an overhead press, all in one continuous cycle with no natural pause.

The classic time-killer is failing after going unbroken too early and then standing around catching your breath. Strategy beats fitness here: many athletes PR simply by splitting the set of 21 into planned blocks (e.g., 12/9 or 11/10) instead of going to failure. Transitions matter too: every second spent standing between the last pull-up and the first thruster of the next round adds up.

## Historical Context Few People Know

Fran was first programmed by Greg Glassman around 2001–2002 and is one of CrossFit's original "Girls" WODs, even though its name doesn't follow that official pattern. The choice of 95/65 lb wasn't arbitrary: it's meant to keep the movement fast and nearly aerobic, not a test of maximal strength. The 21-15-9 scheme is designed so the total volume stays manageable while the accumulated pace is what breaks the athlete.

## What This Calculator Does NOT Include

- **It doesn't predict performance in other WODs**: Fran measures a specific capacity (glycolytic power plus coordination under fatigue). An elite Fran time doesn't guarantee the same level in long-duration WODs or those with heavy weightlifting components.
- **It doesn't adjust for age or training history**: the bands are absolute, not relative to your demographic.
- **It doesn't validate technique**: a 3:00 with partial range-of-motion pull-ups isn't comparable to a clean 3:00.
- **It doesn't replace a coach's assessment**: if you're near the boundary between levels, a video of your execution provides more information than the time alone.

## Common Mistakes When Interpreting Your Result

1. **Comparing Scaled with Rx**: they are different metrics. A 2:30 Scaled and a 2:30 Rx are not equivalent.
2. **Not recording the conditions**: Bar from the rack or the floor? Kipping or strict? First attempt of the day or after a warm-up? Reproducibility depends on standardizing everything.
3. **Retesting too often**: Fran is taxing. Most coaches recommend retesting every **8–12 weeks** at minimum to see real adaptation rather than residual fatigue.
4. **Skipping the warm-up**: unlike long WODs, Fran requires arriving primed. Without a proper warm-up, the first thrusters of the set of 21 slow your total time disproportionately.

## How to Use This Calculator

Enter your most recent time in seconds (300 = 5:00). The calculator returns your current level and the next benchmark to chase. Retest **the same way** — same load, same movement standard, same time of day — so the comparison stays valid.

faq.a: Fran is a benchmark WOD consisting of 21-15-9 reps of 95 lb thrusters and pull-ups, completed for time. It tests strength, power, and cardio capacity in one short workout.
Most CrossFit athletes complete Fran between 4-8 minutes. Elite athletes finish under 2:30. Beginners or scaled versions may take 8-12 minutes.

faq.q: What's considered a good Fran time?
faq.a: A good time is 3:00-4:00. This puts you in the intermediate to advanced category. Elite level is sub-2:30.
Yes. Scaled Fran uses 65 lb thrusters and jumping or assisted pull-ups. There's no shame in scaling—scaling maintains workout intensity while building capacity.

faq.q: How often should I test Fran?
faq.a: Most athletes retest Fran every 3-6 months to track progress. Testing too frequently (weekly) can mask real improvements and increase injury risk.

Popular benchmarks include Cindy (20 min AMRAP of 5 pull-ups, 10 push-ups, 15 squats), Murph (1 mi run, 100 pull-ups, 200 push-ups, 300 squats, 1 mi run), and Helen (3 rounds: 400m run, 21 kettlebell swings, 12 pull-ups).

faq.q: Is my Fran time counted if I don't meet movement standards?
faq.a: In official competitions, reps that don't meet standards (full squat, full elbow extension, chin over bar) don't count. Always prioritize good movement over speed.
